title: Status Page Component Taxonomy (Customer-Facing) — Proposal v1.0
author: Christine Wong
body:
## Overview
This page defines the *customer-facing* status page components for Redwood Inference and provides clear definitions, examples of partial impact, and rules for mapping internal incidents/alerts to public components.

**Goals**
- Improve accuracy: customers can quickly understand *what is impacted* (e.g., Streaming only vs full API).
- Improve actionability: customers can decide whether to retry/backoff, switch models, disable streaming, or pin regions.
- Standardize comms: consistent component selection across oncall rotations.

**Non-goals**
- Exposing internal architecture/service names.
- Publishing sensitive details (provider contracts, customer identities, exploit/vulnerability-like details). See: External Comms Approval Policy.

## Design principles
1) **Customer comprehension over internal fidelity.** Component names should describe what customers experience, not our internal service graph.
2) **Prefer specificity, avoid over-scoping.** If only Streaming is failing, do not mark “Hosted API” degraded.
3) **Use the smallest set of components that fully explains impact.** If multiple customer-visible surfaces are affected, select multiple components.
4) **Separate control plane vs data plane when it changes customer actions.** If provisioning/management is broken but inference is healthy, mark control plane, not serving.
5) **Region scoping is meaningful when it informs routing.** If impact is isolated to a region, use region components.
6) **Avoid internal jargon.** Use “Capacity & Routing” rather than “Scheduler.”

## Component hierarchy (high level)
We group components by product surface area:
- Hosted (API)
- Console
- Dedicated
- Private
- Cross-cutting (Auth, Capacity & Routing)

> Note: The status page UI may display these as a flat list or a parent/child hierarchy depending on vendor capabilities. This taxonomy supports either.

---

## Customer-facing components (v1.0)
Below is the canonical list. Each component includes a definition, typical symptoms, and examples of partial impact.

### 1) Hosted API — Gateway & Authentication
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Gateway & Auth

**Definition:** Entry-point services for request authentication/authorization, rate limiting enforcement, request routing to serving, and request admission.

**Typical symptoms**
- Elevated **401/403** for valid keys
- Elevated **429** beyond expected quota behavior (unintended throttling)
- Elevated **5xx** at the edge (before model execution)
- Requests fail quickly with gateway errors; streaming may not start

**Partial impact examples**
- Only requests using a specific auth mechanism (e.g., signed requests) fail while API keys continue to work.
- Write operations for API keys (rotate/create) fail while inference requests succeed.

**Customer action guidance (commonly included in updates)**
- Validate API key and org; retry with exponential backoff
- If only one region is impacted and customer uses region pinning: route to another region

---

### 2) Hosted API — Chat/Completions (Non-Streaming)
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Chat/Completions

**Definition:** Non-streaming text generation endpoints and synchronous response delivery.

**Typical symptoms**
- Elevated **5xx** on chat/completions endpoints
- Elevated latency / timeouts on non-streaming calls
- Output truncation not attributable to client timeouts

**Partial impact examples**
- Only specific request sizes (long prompts) time out; small prompts succeed.
- Only one model family fails; other models succeed (use Model Family component only if we expose it; see “Model-scoped usage”).

---

### 3) Hosted API — Streaming
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Streaming

**Definition:** Server-sent events / streaming response delivery for chat/completions. Includes connection handling, keepalives, and stream chunk delivery.

**Typical symptoms**
- Increased streaming disconnects or incomplete streams
- Streams start but terminate early
- “connection reset / unexpected EOF” patterns in client logs
- Non-streaming responses remain healthy

**Partial impact examples**
- Streaming fails only for certain client networks while non-streaming works (still mark Streaming if our metrics show elevated disconnect rates).
- Streaming works but has elevated tail latency between chunks; total completion time increases.

**When to select Streaming vs Chat/Completions**
- If *only* streaming delivery is affected and non-streaming success rate is normal: select **Hosted API — Streaming** only.
- If the underlying generation is failing (e.g., 5xx across both streaming and non-streaming): select **Chat/Completions** (and Streaming if streaming-specific failures also exist).

---

### 4) Hosted API — Embeddings
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Embeddings

**Definition:** Embedding generation endpoints.

**Typical symptoms**
- Elevated 5xx on embeddings route(s)
- Elevated latency for embedding responses
- Errors related to input length validation beyond normal behavior

**Partial impact examples**
- One embedding model version has elevated errors while another version remains healthy.
- Large-batch embedding requests fail while small batches succeed.

---

### 5) Hosted API — Rerank
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Rerank

**Definition:** Reranking endpoints used for ranking documents/snippets.

**Typical symptoms**
- Elevated 5xx on rerank routes
- Increased latency and timeouts

**Partial impact examples**
- Only rerank in one region is degraded; embeddings and chat remain healthy.

---

### 6) Hosted API — Capacity & Routing
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Capacity & Routing

**Definition:** Customer-visible capacity constraints and routing behavior affecting request acceptance or model availability. Includes overload protection, admission control, and routing policy issues.

**Typical symptoms**
- Elevated 429/503 due to capacity (beyond expected quota)
- Specific model(s) unavailable or repeatedly failing due to capacity
- Regional imbalance: one region rejects while another serves normally

**Partial impact examples**
- Only a high-demand model family experiences capacity-based rejections.
- Requests succeed but are routed to a fallback model unexpectedly (only mark if it is a platform-side behavior impacting expected service; ensure wording is customer-safe).

**Important disclosure note**
Do **not** describe internal schedulers, GPU vendors, or provider-level causes in detail on the status page. Use customer-safe phrasing like “capacity constraints in <region> for <feature>.”

---

### 7) Hosted API — Region: us-east
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Serving (us-east)

**Definition:** Region-specific serving health for hosted inference in **us-east**.

**Typical symptoms**
- Increased 5xx/latency isolated to us-east
- Capacity errors limited to us-east

**Partial impact examples**
- Only us-east has elevated errors for embeddings; other regions remain normal.

**When to use**
- Use region components when impact is isolated to that region *and* customers can meaningfully route away.
- If multiple regions are impacted or root cause is global, prefer global components (e.g., Chat/Completions, Streaming) and mention affected regions in the incident text.

---

### 8) Hosted API — Region: us-west
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Serving (us-west)

(See “Region: us-east” for definition and usage.)

---

### 9) Hosted API — Region: eu-west
**Customer label:** Hosted API — Serving (eu-west)

(See “Region: us-east” for definition and usage.)

---

### 10) Redwood Console
**Customer label:** Console

**Definition:** Web UI and console-backed APIs for usage analytics, rollouts, keys management (UI surface), and operational dashboards.

**Typical symptoms**
- Console pages fail to load, elevated 5xx
- Usage dashboards stale or unavailable
- Rollout/traffic split UI actions fail

**Partial impact examples**
- Console is down but Hosted API continues to serve.
- Token/cost breakdown is delayed while other console functionality works.

---

### 11) Dedicated — Control Plane
**Customer label:** Dedicated — Control Plane

**Definition:** Dedicated cluster provisioning, configuration, scaling controls, and management APIs (customer’s reserved capacity management layer).

**Typical symptoms**
- Cannot scale or modify dedicated capacity settings
- Provisioning operations fail
- Management API returns 5xx while inference still works

**Partial impact examples**
- Customers cannot change autoscaling policies but existing workloads continue successfully.

---

### 12) Dedicated — Serving
**Customer label:** Dedicated — Serving

**Definition:** Runtime serving path for customers on Dedicated capacity.

**Typical symptoms**
- Elevated 5xx/latency for Dedicated endpoints
- Model loading failures affecting Dedicated customers

**Partial impact examples**
- Only one dedicated fleet/cluster is impacted (do not name customers; scope by region or “subset of Dedicated capacity” in text).

---

### 13) Private — Control Plane
**Customer label:** Private — Control Plane

**Definition:** Management services for Redwood Private (VPC / on-prem) that affect admin operations, updates, telemetry (where applicable), and policy configuration.

**Typical symptoms**
- Private management operations failing (config updates, rollouts)
- Console integrations for Private unavailable

**Partial impact examples**
- Control plane operations fail while in-VPC inference remains healthy.

---

### 14) Private — Serving
**Customer label:** Private — Serving

**Definition:** Serving runtime health for Private deployments where Redwood is responsible for the runtime and/or managed upgrades.

**Typical symptoms**
- Elevated errors/latency for Private inference endpoints

**Partial impact examples**
- Only a subset of Private customers on a specific runtime version are impacted (keep wording generic; do not reveal customer list).

---

## Model-scoped usage (optional / controlled)
We generally avoid public components per model family to prevent a long list and reduce confusion. However, during an incident, it may be valuable to specify model scope *in the incident text*.

**Allowed in incident text (customer-safe):**
- “Impacts requests to the <model name> family” (if the model name is already public in our catalog)
- “Impacts a subset of models” when we cannot confidently scope further

**Avoid:**
- Internal model IDs, canary fleet names, GPU type references, or capacity provider details.

---

## Mapping rules (internal → public)
These rules are intended to be applied by oncall and incident-bot prompts.

### Rule A — Choose components based on customer-observable impact
Select components based on:
- Endpoint/feature affected (Streaming vs Embeddings vs Rerank)
- Surface area affected (Console vs API)
- Deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
- Region scope (us-east/us-west/eu-west)

Do **not** select components purely because an internal service paged.

### Rule B — Use multiple components when customers would experience multiple failures
Examples:
- Elevated 401/403 + normal serving once authenticated → **Gateway & Auth** only.
- Auth OK but streaming disconnects elevated → **Streaming** only.
- Streaming disconnects + increased model 5xx → **Streaming** and **Chat/Completions**.
- Console down + Hosted API healthy → **Console** only.

### Rule C — Prefer “Streaming” over “Chat/Completions” for streaming-only delivery failures
If model execution success is normal but stream transport is failing, mark **Streaming**.

### Rule D — Region components are additive, not mandatory
- If the issue is isolated to a region and actionable for customers: use **Hosted API — Serving (<region>)** in addition to the relevant global functional component(s) *only if it improves clarity*.
- If adding region components would confuse (e.g., multiple regions flapping): mark the functional component(s) globally and list affected regions in the update text.

### Rule E — Capacity constraints should map to “Capacity & Routing” when not explained by quotas
- If errors are due to customer quota enforcement behaving as designed, do not open an incident.
- If there is unintended throttling, elevated 503/429 due to platform capacity, or routing instability: select **Capacity & Routing**.

### Rule F — Control plane vs serving
- Provisioning/configuration failures but inference ok → **Control Plane**.
- Inference errors/latency → **Serving**.
- If both are impacted, select both.

---

## Quick examples (component selection)
1) **Streaming-only keepalive timeout in us-east**
- Components: Hosted API — Streaming; Hosted API — Serving (us-east)
- Avoid: Hosted API — Chat/Completions (unless non-streaming is also impacted)

2) **Embeddings 5xx across all regions**
- Components: Hosted API — Embeddings
- Text: mention “all regions” (no region components needed)

3) **Console dashboards stale, API healthy**
- Components: Console

4) **Dedicated management API failing, inference still ok**
- Components: Dedicated — Control Plane

5) **Capacity rejections for one high-demand public model in eu-west**
- Components: Hosted API — Capacity & Routing; Hosted API — Serving (eu-west)
- Text: “Requests to <public model name> in eu-west may receive 503/429 due to capacity constraints.”

---

## Operational notes
**Status page component changes require:**
- Incident-bot configuration updates (prompts + allowed component IDs)
- Signal coverage validation (each component must have at least one reliable metric/alert)
- Docs updates (“How to read our status page”)

**Ownership (initial)**
- Taxonomy steward / changes: Rafael Mendes
- Console component naming: Marissa Cole (consult)
- Public docs alignment: Elliot Price
- Disclosure checks: Dr. Aisha Rahman / Olga Petrov (as needed)

---

## Change log
- **2024-07-02:** Published v1.0 with “Capacity & Routing” naming (replacing internal ‘Scheduler’ terminology) and explicit separation of Dedicated/Private control plane vs serving.
- **2024-06-18:** Added explicit Streaming component and region serving components (us-east/us-west/eu-west) based on recurring support escalations.

## Open questions (tracked in Linear epic)
- Whether to add a separate component for “Model Catalog / Model Availability” vs using “Capacity & Routing” + incident text.
- Whether to add additional regions as we expand (APAC) and how to present them without overwhelming customers.
